On a high-level, we can expect the following ([thread|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06JWDKDHT8/p1726150422476499?thread_ts=1725349872.360079&cid=C06JWDKDHT8]):

*Riders* (shouldn't have too many questions/concerns)

* General questions about Bidding (What it is, Why I have to do it, How do I go back to the previous model, etc.)
- We'll address this with the FAQs and Tutorial Videos/Blog Posts
* General usage questions (Why can't I go higher/lower with the price, Driver offers got vanished etc.)
- We'll address this with the FAQs and Tutorial Videos
* Riders complaining about drivers often increasing the prices (drivers can do a counter-offer to the rider)
* Riders complaining that it is taking much longer to find a driver (maybe they're reducing the price, which can be up to -10% of the base price)
* Riders complaining that the driver didn't turn on the AC or being rude (maybe the driver was unhappy about getting matched at -10% price)
* Riders asking how they can skip bidding UX
- Riders who don't want to engage in bidding can choose to go with the suggested price and enable "auto-match" so that we automatically match the first driver who accepts their offer

*Drivers* (should have relatively more questions compared to the rider)

* General questions about bidding and usage (like how x works or what y means)
- e.g. How to edit the price? i.e. a custom input outside of the suggested options
* Drivers complaining that they aren't getting B2B rides now (back-to-back rides)
- The MVP doesn't have it
* Drivers complaining about riders lowballing them
- Shouldn't be a big deal as the riders can't go below -10%
* Drivers complaining that they don't like waiting for riders to pick the driver
- Something we have to deal with for now. As more riders adopt auto-match, it should be the same as the current experience as long as they don't send a counter-offer
- In the future, drivers can set auto-acceptance rules which will make the experience seamless
   - This will address another concern that drivers have to spend extra time scrutinizing ride prices
* Drivers asking whether the price includes surge
- The answer is "Yes"
- We still suggest the same price to the riders as we do today. The can only go -10% to +30% on it.
* Drivers complaining about [blast dispatch|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/CSPROGMNG-341] (the same request sent to 5-7 drivers at once)
- They might be concerned that the offer disappears even before they could accept it (don't think it'll happen that quickly, but can totally happen - especially, if these drivers are in the second rounding of matching)
* Drivers asking about the commission % and whether increasing the price impacts it in anyway

No seguimento da nossa meeting ontem, deixo só aqui anotado o que discutimos, caso precisemos destas informações mais tarde.

* *Sobre os casos que vêm de tribunais (o que também inclui casos de julgados de paz):* não é necessário pedir base legal desde que o pedido pareça ser justificado e proporcional. Enquanto não está mais explícito no KB, se tivermos alguma dúvida, podemos criar um jira sobre o caso em questão, para a legal team poder ir entendendo quais são os casos e dar-nos indicação de que podemos prosseguir com a resposta.
* *Casos de ofício com base legal:* não é necessário termos o artigo específico, apenas citar a lei é suficiente. Se houver uma lei diferente das leis que estão no KB, criar jira para confirmar se é válido (pensando também em atualizar a lista se necessário).
* *Quando não localizamos a informação com os dados fornecidos*: tentar mostrar colaboração total. Tipo ‘podem dar mais algum dado para que possamos procurar pela informação desejada''.
* *Quando solicitamos mais alguma informação e a authority não responde em 5 dias*: a KB diz para enviarmos uma resposta. Essa resposta seria desnecessária uma vez que a authority não tem um prazo para nos enviar a resposta. Sendo assim, pode ser fechado com uma nota interna e não enviar uma nova resposta.
* *Em casos de fraude em que nos fornecem dados do cartão* (sem a data de validade, por exemplo), mas que nós conseguimos localizar as informações com os dados fornecidos, não temos necessidade de pedir a data de validade (mesmo estando na KB). Por enquanto, podemos criar um SD nesses casos para confirmar que podemos enviar, caso necessário. Entretanto, será verificado se existe alguma base legal para essa solicitação.

Tested in *Android* prelive with the following:

# USER1 logged into RH (+37270000502)
# USER2 logged into BF (+37270000500)
# Close BF from app carousel (not force quit from OS settings)
# Opened BF back and saw Cross App Login Modal for USER1 (the one on RH)



These are the [Kibana logs|https://kibana-logs.prelive.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/r?l=DISCOVER_APP_LOCATOR&v=8.13.4&%2BBKG4ywLMs5i%2Fhcxx3AAKgsqyIHcByIEexiHhcABaCQgnBCFIQsKFGOhmGIAcWF7LwFwHIeJFBt60HJMMt5sH8AIbv8uTSoeCxiQstjyBACqIJy0A1kAA%3D%3D&auth_provider_hint=anonymous1]. The problem is with how the app state call is made from the client:


!image-20240913-093722.png|width=1385,height=206,alt="image-20240913-093722.png"!

❗  *phone* is  +37270000500 (used in BF), but *auth_username* is +37270000502 (used in RH).

* The login session in BF is created for { phone number = +37270000500 and phone_uuid = e7…} 
* after BF app open the app state call is made with inconsistent phone and auth_username params. The app state in backend is made to prioritise {{auth_username}} over {{phone}} param. So when the app is reopened we check { auth_username = +37270000502 and phone_uuid = e7…, auth_token taken from RH} and see there’s no active session for this pair of credentials and the auth token taken from RH is valid for USER1 so we enable cross-app login with USER1

*Case:*

* User has a Bolt balance of 10 EUR.
* A booking is created for 10.10 EUR.
* 10 EUR is covered by the balance.
* The remaining 0.10 EUR is attempted to be charged from the provided payment instrument.
* The payment system rejects the transaction with a {{PAYMENT_AMOUNT_TOO_LOW}} error (due to the {{payment_minimal_amount}} config).



*Options to fix:*

*Option 1:*

* Take less from the balance, for example, 9 EUR.
* Make a larger card payment for 1.10 EUR.

*Pros:*

* The booking succeeds. :)

*Cons:*

* The user will have a confusing 1 EUR balance remaining and might wonder why it wasn’t used in full.
* The booking system needs knowledge of the {{payment_minimal_amount}} config.



*Option 2:*

* Ignore {{PAYMENT_AMOUNT_TOO_LOW}} errors at the booking level for authorizations and captures.
* The user will have a 10-cent debt that will be covered with the next order.

*Pros:*

* The booking succeeds.
* This is the easiest option to implement.
* Bolt saves money by avoiding transaction fees for very small payments.

*Cons:*

* Seeing a small debt might be alarming to the user.



*Option 3:*

* Treat the leftover 10 cents as a discount.

*Pros:*

* The booking succeeds.
* Bolt avoids paying transaction fees for very small payments.
* This offers the best user experience.

*Cons:*

* This is the most complex option to implement and requires further technical discussions (either from the vertical level or somehow from the commerce side).
* Bolt would have to write off these small amounts.

After some technical usage of GPs ([here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MARTECH-6072]), here are some usage opportunities that we see:

*Interpreting 100% (or most of) Android/iOS differences as impact of ads*

* GPs can fit lots of different processes, but fitting any process is not generalizeable. The only opportunity to use such results is as ‘confidence intervals’ - upper and lower bound of impact of ads. But these patterns are not necessarily repeatable, so it’s more complicated to incorporate this idea to budgeting.

*Seasonality*

* The only other generalizeable (and therefore usable) opportunity to use the idea time-varying impact is *seasonality* (i.e. repeatable patterns) - annual, monthly or weekly. 
* However, seasonality seems to be some pattern that is often complicated to find and confirm within one model - there’s often not much evidence. What is more Android/iOS relation can be varying even without ads (i.e. just data from Android/iOS might not be enough to be sure that the differences are produced by ads). Therefore, I’d suggest that we:
** Try to show and reconstruct seasonality as some ground truth relevant across not just one model, but larger span of data. (i.e. we would try to deduce seasonality *EITHER* on one market, but across larger historic span than one year *OR* on multiple markets that we consider similar *OR* on all markets.
** We will try to employ not just data from Android/iOS differences (which might be rather noisy, but also employ other data that can indirectly give signals about varying ads effectiveness. Those could be:
*** Impressions to clicks conversion data (very upper funnel)
*** Install or FTR attribution data (signups not available)
*** Android / IOS differences data (is least open to the signal, but could probably work as confirmation)
* Note that different seasonalities have different usages:
** Annual seasonality - impacts Budgeting
** Monthly and weekly - impacts settings in business managers (but not budgeting, done on annual or quarterly levels)

Hey [~accountid:6149a0e9ba1b34006ab04897] just jumping in from a product legal POV:

* the DSA (European Digital Service Act, not data sharing agreement) requires platforms to collect and display more information about traders to users (Art. 30 DSA). The DSA also applies to Bolt as a platform. We have found some compromises on the displaying part but it looks like the Spanish team has in general also the issue with collecting those documents. 

* we have already received in other countries regulatory requests about this topic.
* the risk of non complying with the DSA can be 6% of the annual global GMV of Bolt.
* I understand that in Spain the compliance level is nearly zero and blocking if existing supply does not have any documents by the 15th of February 2025 could have a significant business impact.
* we’d suggest to flag the risk to your local stakeholders and map out the onboarding process for supply of our competitors in the market. Worth checking what Uber is requesting from Fleets to go online on their platform.

He requested the *trips between the 10/18/2023 and 10/20/2023.*

{{Case 1 - Fraud flagged counts}}

_Problem:_ 

We are currently counting all in fraud flags regardless of the payment method in {{query.driver.extended_order_statistics.week.fraud_orders_count}} and this results in us involving cases of cash activity, for which, we often have no way to ‘save’ through payout checks. Cash orders does not result in driver positive balance movements (unless there is a campaign adjustment/app payment). This means that we highlight a lot mixed cases where drivers only conduct one payment type of fraud but their ‘earnings’ for payout as such do not correlate to the fraud they do. Hence, as a result the payout checks are not efficient and will not offer savings but will cost resources and affect ‘good’ money. 

Further, the name {{fraud_orders_count}} is currently misleading as it doesn't count orders that have flags but fraud flags.

_Approx impact:_ 

Average {color:#bf2600}*3K eur weekly / 12K eur monthly*{color} impact of money handled through checks + operationally average 1h less work weekly or 4h less work monthly

In case we opt for splits, it will help up target better fraud which we currently could not catch due to all flags being in one pot. E.g we can be more aggressive towards drivers who have mixed volumes of GMV but only do fraud on in-app (or business payment methods). 

Opportunity in 6 month period where at least 50% of the in-app sum was fraud flagged (and not refunded through profiling) and it was a mixed volume driver. This makes roughly {color:#bf2600}*17K eur extra monthly*{color} impact we could check more accurately in payouts.

SELECT 
y.country,
sum(y.sum_inapp_orders_with_flags__not_refunded) AS sum_not_refunded,
sum(y.sum_inapp_orders_with_flags) AS sum_total_inapp_fraud_flagged
FROM (
WITH stats AS(
		--
		SELECT 
			x.driver_id,
			date_trunc('week',x.created) AS week_stats,
			count(x.order_id) AS count_orders,
			count(CASE WHEN x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN x.order_id END) AS count_inapp_orders,
			count(CASE WHEN x.payment_method_group = 'cash' THEN x.order_id END) AS count_cash_orders,
			sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS count_trips_with_flags,
			sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)*1.00/NULLIF(count(x.order_id),0) AS ratio_count_flagged_trips,
			sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS count_inapp_trips_with_flags,
			COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)*1.00/NULLIF(count(CASE WHEN x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN x.order_id END),0),0) AS ratio_inapp_count_flagged_trips,
			sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'cash' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS count_cash_trips_with_flags,
			COALESCE(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'cash' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)*1.00/NULLIF(count(CASE WHEN x.payment_method_group = 'cash' THEN x.order_id END),0),0) AS ratio_count_cash_flagged_trips,
			round(sum(x.user_price_eur),0) AS sum_orders,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN x.user_price_eur END),0),0) AS sum_inapp_orders,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.payment_method_group = 'cash' THEN x.user_price_eur END),0),0) AS sum_cash_orders,
			round(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0) AS sum_orders_with_flags,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(sum(x.user_price_eur),0),2),0) AS ratio_sum_flagged_trips,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0) AS sum_inapp_orders_with_flags,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND (x.refund_amount = 0 OR x.refund_amount IS NULL) AND x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0) AS sum_inapp_orders_with_flags__not_refunded,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(sum(CASE WHEN x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN x.user_price_eur END),0),2),0) AS ratio_sum_inapp_flagged_trips,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'in-app' THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),2),0) AS ratio_sum_inapp_from_all_flagged,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'cash' THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END),0),0) AS sum_cash_orders_with_flags,
			COALESCE(round(sum(CASE WHEN x.count_flags > 0 AND x.payment_method_group = 'cash' THEN x.user_price_eur ELSE 0 END)/NULLIF(sum(CASE WHEN x.payment_method_group = 'cash' THEN x.user_price_eur END),0),2),0) AS ratio_sum_cash_flagged_trips
			FROM (
				SELECT 
				co.created AS created,
				co.order_id,
				co.country_code AS country_code,
				co.user_id AS user_id,
				co.driver_courier_id AS driver_id,
				co.user_price_eur,
				co.payment_method_group,
				co.refund_amount,
				approx_distinct(CASE WHEN facr.is_fraud IS NOT NULL THEN facr.id END,0.0041) AS count_flags
				FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS co
				LEFT JOIN ng_public.fraud_order_check as foc ON foc.city_id=co.city_id AND foc.order_id=co.order_id AND foc.user_id=co.user_id AND foc.city_id = co.city_id AND DATE(co.created) = DATE (foc.created) AND date(foc.created_date_hour) >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -2, CURRENT_DATE) AS date)
				LEFT JOIN ng_public.fraud_order_check_result as facr ON facr.order_check_id=foc.id AND date(facr.created_date) >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -2, CURRENT_DATE) AS date)
				WHERE co.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -2, CURRENT_DATE) AS date)
				AND co.order_type ='rides' 
				AND co.order_state = 'finished' 
				AND co.country_code IN ('ke', 'ng', 'gh', 'ug', 'tz', 'ua', 'fr', 'za', 'th', 'az', 'ge', 'lv', 'ee', 'lt')
				GROUP BY 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
			) AS x
			--WHERE x.driver_id = 3853271
			GROUP BY 1,2
		)
		SELECT
		DISTINCT pp.id AS payout_id,
				date_trunc('week',pp.created) AS created_week_payout,
				date_diff('day',s.week_stats,date_trunc('week',pp.created)) AS diff_created_sanity_check,
				s.week_stats AS created_week_orders,
				ca.country,
				pp.client_id,
				pc.external_id AS driver_id,
				s.*,
				pp.created_date AS creation_date_payout,
				pp.amount AS amount,
				pp.currency AS currency,
				round(pp.amount /r.rate,0) AS payout_eur,
				pp."method" AS method,
				pp.state AS state,
				pp."type" AS TYPE
					FROM  glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_payout AS pp
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client AS pc ON pp.client_id = pc.id
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_payout.invoicing_payment_client_account AS ca ON pp.client_id = ca.client_id 
					LEFT JOIN glue.ng_public.vw_currency_exchange_rates r ON r.currency = pp.currency AND date(r.valid_on) = date(pp.created)
					LEFT JOIN stats AS s 
							ON pc.external_id = s.driver_id 
							AND
							date(s.week_stats) = date(date_trunc('week',pp.created)) - INTERVAL '7' DAY
		WHERE 
		pp."method" = 'regular'
		AND 
		pp."type" = 'ride_hailing_driver'
		AND
		pp.state = 'finished'
		AND
		ca.country IN ('ke', 'ng', 'gh', 'ug', 'tz', 'ua', 'fr', 'za', 'th', 'az', 'ge', 'lv', 'ee', 'lt')
		--AND pc.external_id = 2074726
		AND pp.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -1, CURRENT_DATE) AS date)
		--ORDER BY 2 DESC 
		AND s.sum_inapp_orders_with_flags__not_refunded > 10
		AND s.ratio_sum_inapp_flagged_trips >= 0.4
		AND ratio_sum_inapp_from_all_flagged >= 0.1
) AS y
GROUP BY 1{noformat}

Thank you for escalating to Customer Payments team. The customers don't always have a great visibility when the pre-authorization has been returned to them. Returning the pre-authorization is not something Bolt has much control over. 
Depending on the bank the pre-authorization charges can take up to a month to be returned to the customer. 
If the Authorization state is Captured then everything is fine on our side and the customer has to check with their bank. 

Please only escalate the issue to Payment Operations team if

1. The funds have not been returned after 30 days and customer has checked with their bank

2. The state has been stuck in authorization for more than 24 hours. (72h for Micro Mobility) 

3. The state of the authorization is failed or error. 

Please leave a comment on the ticket if you still want it to be escalated to the Customer Payments team. Else the ticket will be closed in 5 days.

{quote}The whole process is not free for a server. If you check the CPU utilization, you will see that the “mirroring” in ProxySQL actually doubles the CPU utilization. This means that the traffic on server A is impacted because of resource contention.

Summarizing, ProxySQL will:

# Send the query for execution in different order
# Completely ignore any transaction isolation
# Have different number of query executed on B with respect to A
# Add significant load on the server resources

[~accountid:5bdbfc9b359ddf204e8c7e02] according to the wording of the clause in the Alcohol Act, a violation of age verification does not permit an initial “warning” before imposing a monetary fine. Thus, if the violation occurs, a monetary fine will be imposed in addition to a request to remedy the infringement. Before determining the amount of the fine, authorities will request us to provide an explanation. The fine will depend on the strength of our arguments to demonstrate what measures were taken to ensure proper age verification. However, it is entirely at the discretion of the authorities to assess the strength of our arguments and then set the fine accordingly.

When determining the fine, the authorities typically consider the following factors:

* _Nature and gravity of the infringement:_ how serious the infringement was. Selling alcohol to minors or failing to verify age can have significant public health and safety implications.
* _Duration and frequency of the violation:_ whether it was a one-time event or a systematic failure. If the company repeatedly fails to verify the age of customers or has been doing so over a prolonged period, the fine may be higher.
* _Intent or negligence:_ deliberate actions typically result in higher penalties.
* _Cooperation:_ If a company cooperates with authorities and takes immediate steps to prevent future violations, this could lead to a reduced penalty.
* _Size and financial situation:_ larger companies may face higher fines to ensure the penalty acts as an adequate deterrent.
* _Previous offenses:_ If there have been previous similar violations, the fine could be increased (I think we dont have such cases)
* _Public interest and harm:_ the broader impact of the violation on public health, particularly regarding minors, and the harm caused to society.

Fines are imposed not only as a punishment but also to deter future violations.

Also clarified Okai test report with [~accountid:6215e9f275803500683497d5] :   

* Report text and graphs are difficult to understand
* I understood that same phase mosfets were in conductive state wrongly so that current could flow directly between battery + and - and cause little short circuit which would heat mosfets
* Carrier / Switching frequency was lowered to reduce switching losses (less switching per time period). It can make motor more noisy, seems biggest negative effect.
* *Deadband time should be longer, not shorter* - like described in report. Making it longer gives more time to switch off upper and turn on lower mosfet for example - so they would not ON at the same time and cause short circuit.
* Lower modulation ratio - motor voltage compared to battery voltage ratio. It might reduce heat generation but also reduce top speed.
* Efficiency drop 2% - *might also mean range drop 2%*.
* MOS drive minimum voltage - might mean that mosfet OFF state meant having 0V at gate terminal, now it is 5,2V. (ON state has higher voltage). If this is true, might reduce switching losses and heat.

The reason for HW failures is mostly detected as MOSFET traces burning due to overheating. Once it has happened the controller will not be operable.

*Solution:* OKAI developed a new FW which should prevent the controller to have this failure and turn to protection mode before it can damage the HW mode any further. The logic is that when the controller with new FW detects the temperature is near critical, it will trigger the protection and the new display FW will show an *error code “31”* indicating that it is in protection mode. Once the Controller temperature drops below ~80 degrees Celsius, it will automatically return to normal mode.

On Dragon controllers we would not accept these issues. If we will not get improvements by Okai and only order option will be this controller, have to perform live testing with smaller quantity.

OKAI is working on a software fix for an issue they think is the root cause for the failures

Explanation from Mr. Andy (16.11.2022):

* _First - Root cause analysised by OKAI: When scooter is moving with current output, and same time there is big load, ECU temperature will goes up to an unbearable range and damage the MOSFET.  This usually happens when the temperature is high and climbing a hill._

       _Solution for this cause: Firmware, this FW is for stopping the motor when the ECU is overheated._ *NOTE:* *THIS FW upgrade is already deployed, we have seen little effect.*

* _Second - Root cause analysised by OKAI:  When the scooter is moving under high current, the duty ratio of some ECU is over modulated and the main manifestation is that the upper and lower MOSFETs pulse width is narrow, in this case the MOSFET can't be opened completely and causes its burn._

       _Solution - Use software to adjust carrier frequency and modulation ratio to change the pulse width and let Mosfet open freely.   Also this solution is able to readuce the ECU temperature around 10 ℃ which is beneficial._ *ETA by Mr. Andy, 25.11.2022*

# Repair of deep discharged/unresponsive Okai batteries: This task is a bit more complex as it requires the removal of the battery core, and some investigation. Please, talk to Ilvestments about this task and see what they can tell us about it.
# Battery body replacement: We will order new battery shells, and for this activity the top cap need to be removed, then the battery core must be pressed out of the damaged cell, then pressed back into the new sheel (same task when repairing the deep discharged batteries in item 3). While analyzing these scooters I’ve found a pattern where vehicles were showing multiple error like E3, E4, E7 and E8. These errors are related to brake position or brake sensors and throttle position errors. All these three components are connected directly to the display, and after investigating the Hardware and Software versions I’ve found an interesting pattern.
The Display HW is version CF, and according to Okai the latest version of Firmware should be CF for ES400 and ES600.
In Berlin, the fleet is already running running FW CF, and below we have the DNS feedbacks for the last 90 days (top green line):

!Stockholm DNS 90 days.png|width=838,height=509,alt="Stockholm DNS 90 days.png"!

Based on this finding, it was asked to the Tech Core team to update the FW in the whole fleet in Stockholm to version CF.

We are still unsure if this can be influencing the recent increase in DNS feedback, but updating to the latest version now will rule out this hypothesis going forward.

Quick debrief on where we are on the topic of *excessively wearing battery connectors*.

* From our Stockholm analysis, we saw from our diagnosed scooters (on which we were able to recreate the phenomena), that *at least 72%* (others need further diagnosis, but battery connectors CAN NOT be ruled out) of these scooters had GTULF caused directly by bad battery communication - connectors were the root cause.
* The root cause of these connectors wearing is excessive battery vibration in the battery compartment, mostly caused by the bad performance of the GEN2 battery lock and also it is a pitfall of the exposed battery design.
** Solution is to rework all the locks to GEN3 and replace all the worn battery female and scooter male connectors during that.
** OKAI is working on a schedule for reworking to be confirmed as soon as possible, so that Bolt can rework all the locks to GEN3 during the off-season.
** Parts needed for this procedure will need to be manufactured by OKAI and the timeline will be confirmed soon. [~accountid:5f896ba2e357dd006e937e5b] please specify if we have confirmed the timelines and all will be provided as agreed upon.
* OKAI is also working on a better battery connector design for future, but it will not be usable by us for the rework, as they are still developing and testing it.

Both torque sensors were tested, focusing primarily on speed and torque outputs, and test rides were conducted with both sensors.

h3. Speed sensor

I tested the speed sensors by rotating the axis with an electric drill at maximum speed and measuring the output signal. Although the exact RPM of the axis wasn’t known, both tests had the same input speed, making them comparable.

* *Bafang Sensor* (Picture 1):
** Frequency: ~770 Hz
** Positive Duty Cycle: ~60.8%
** Peak-to-Peak Voltage: 3.3V
** Signal: Clean and square
* *LDS Sensor* (Picture 2):
** Frequency: ~745 Hz
** Positive Duty Cycle: ~59.2%
** Peak-to-Peak Voltage: 4V
** Signal: Square wave with 0.2V oscillation on the high side

The primary concern is the LDS sensor’s higher voltage output.

|!Bafang_speed.png|width=869,height=477,alt="Bafang_speed.png"!|!LDS_speed.png|width=868,height=479,alt="LDS_speed.png"!|
|Picture 1. Bafang sensor speed output|Picture 2. LDS sensor speed output|

h3. Torque sensor

I evaluated the torque sensors by fixing the back wheel, applying pressure to the crank arm, and measuring the torque sensor output voltage. I performed four tests: without weight, with 10 kg, with 20 kg, and with 30 kg weight. To compare with the datasheet, I calculated the torque using a crank arm length of 172 mm.
There is a slight difference in the torque sensor output voltages; the LDS sensor output is higher for the same applied torque.

!https://lh7-qw.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXdK-NJh0IJf_SwkVtR0CpnjcxtD05Sev_ZDPaLSgHql7gZFA23QZDvKZXDVuof_ZzLdYwadpHgiPJiSSmkZa4miuSaBTivhLKrUBkgiqjF62k9F5kWFCY2e1vVT0g1b6niLLQH9-E5PBJKB0_zWtEYtuSzt?key=Udvi06oLwuSAdwOVZMw-BA|width=100%!

Picture 3. Torque sensor graphs

h3. Ride test

Both ride tests felt normal and safe. During the LDS ride test, I reached speeds of 29 km/h, whereas with the Bafang sensor, the speed was up to 25 km/h.

h2. Conclusion

The specific signals used by the controller from the torque sensor are not known, but it appears that the LDS torque sensor cannot be used as a direct replacement, because bike reached 29 km/h when riding. The controller firmware will need adjustments to use the new torque sensor.

This was caused by the scooters falling on the left side brake lever and thus shattering the very fragile bell lever which supports the bell and attaches the lever to the bracket. If these broke, the bell shaft shattered and brake lever could no more be used.

After talking to the mechanics and some internal discussions within our team of FAEs, the common understanding is the main problem is the shaft and not the bell. When hitting the floor, the brake lever transfers shear force to the axle breaking it. Usually, the bells remain intact after the impact, and the axle is damaged.
In Switzerland, mechanics were able to drill an M5 hole in damaged bells, installing a regular bolt as an axle. The bolts are much stronger than the sintered axle and can resist the impact when hitting the floor. The process was posted [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02QY814GMA/p1706003839755479].
If we can procure bells with M5 threads on them, we can drastically increase the number of functional vehicles after a drop, by keeping the brakes fully functional. If the bell ever gets damaged, even the Field Operators will be able to replace it on the streets.

# It is important to note that Okai ES600 vehicles are designed to operate between 0° and 40° according to the specification.
# The Swedish team in Stockholm and Gothenburg reported similar issues but also reported that Gen3 locks are less prone to this failure.
# Okai suggested drilling a draining hole in the bottom part of the controller, at the same location where the Lock Motors Gen3 has it, to improve drainage. However, the scooter must be disassembled to perform this action.
# During talks with local teams, it was suggested to apply silicone spray on the top of the motor (locking pin), helping to repeal the water.
# Performed a simple test in Tallinn to assess how effective the silicone could be, taking a motor lock from a scooter (outside temperature -5°C):
## After applying water over the lock motor and letting it outside for 2h, it freezes and does not work. The lock motor works again when the water melts down (around 10 min).
## A generous amount of silicone was applied twice, allowing drying time in between, and the test was repeated. Same result.
## The drainage hole was drilled, and the test was repeated. Same result.
## Silicone was reapplied from the top and in the drainage hole, but the results remained the same.
## CONCLUSION: The silicone might help to repeal the water, but further testing is required to assess its effectiveness.
# The German team was suggested to test drilling a drainage hole through the battery shell in locks Gen2 to see if the situation improves. The hardware Team is working closely with the German team to find a practical solution.
Okai supplied a couple of IPX7-rated lock motors for testing. Bolt’s Supply Chain Team will order a few Gen2 and Gen3 lock motors samples for testing in a salt spray camera.

Recently, we didn’t have more reports of this issue from LOPS. The locks are being replaced with Gen3 Locks, and Okai is designing an IPX7 lock motor to mitigate this issue if necessary. After drilling a drainage hole in Gen2 Lock motors, mechanics in Porto report a noticeable decrease in unlocking failure.

A process for winterization was suggested by Alcino Major. It consists in drilling the lock without removing it from the vehicle, and injecting lithium grease into the gearing mechanism.

As of now, a test has been conducted comparing three different groups:

# Original lock motors, dry (control group)
# Original lock motors, soaked in warm water
# Winterized lock motors, soaked in warm water

The locks are being frozen to sub-zero temperatures overnight, quickly removed from the freezer, and immediately operated to check the functionality.

A center punch tool will be used to “shake” the internal in case the lock motor does not respond, to verify the efficacy of this method also.

*Root cause -* bad battery lock design which:

* collects water in the locking mechanism compartment (condensation, bad sealing) 
* mechanically allows the battery to rattle and vibrate mechanically when it should be fixed sturdily instead
* very difficult to release battery in dire situations as there is no way to mechanically release the battery, so a lot must be disassembled to release the battery and start troubleshooting.

*Short-term:*

There is nothing to be done in current cases but to release the battery by unscrewing the battery lock completely from underneath the scooter and letting the lock drop down so that the battery can be ejected. The lock should then be troubleshooted by mechanics and necessary parts need to be replaced.

*Long-term:* GEN3 lock, which:

* has greatly improved design wise - better mechanical properties, much sturdier design, better logic behind the mechanism
* is keeping the battery fixed in the slot with minimal vibrations/rattling
* has a drainage hole in the bottom for excess water to flow out
* has a mechanical release cable attached to the tongue, routed to the bottom footwell as a failsafe so that the mechanics can easily release batteries.

Issue addressed in [ES600 FAQ document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bKXvNh3PLmKEUuO3RtYTe7C9UZuL-wfP2-uL8mx8dTo/edit]

Discussion point we had during meeting - double wall on frame vs battery compartment generates channel for cables.


* If we have double wall:
** increases frame strength - but this should be validated with simulation if this gives any notable effect
** more complicated frame
** heavier frame - minimal weight gain but still
* If we have compartment plastic to generate channel for cables:
** more design freedom since its moulded part although mould can be complicated
** good access to cable if compartment is removed
** Cable must be fixed - otherwise it is easy to damage cables while inserting compartment plastic
** Could make smaller frame tube since we only have one wall - compartment plastic wall if we would have wall in frame then there is frame wall thickness+compartment plastic wall thickness
!image-20240807-132331.png|width=27.609962904080547%,alt="image-20240807-132331.png"!

About road bikes q-factor.

One of the road bike models made by [+*Pinarello*+ |https://pinarello.com/global/en/bikes/road/competition/new-dogma-f/new-dogma-f-dura-ace-di2#geometrie_anchor]is using *Shimano Dura Ace FC-R9200, HollowTech 2 x12s* crankset. Q-factor on the crankset is *148mm.*
[~accountid:5e46575fc8ec310c955b0d4a] what is the usual Q-factor of citybikes? What would be your preference for the Q-factor?

Q-factor probably varies a lot. In city e-bike category we should not go over 200mm. *Okai EB100 = 240mm, Lime 26in bike = 200, Dolly = 180.* It would be top notch to say that we have Pinarello road bike quality ergonomics, part of it at least although Pinarello is completely different competition category. I am quite sure that because of fixed chainline on the rear motor we never achieve 148mm Q-factor if we want to have straight chain.  On the pedal bikes category q-factors seem to be close to 180mm. *Arcade = 180, MB1=180*,  We should target {color:#36b37e}*180mm q-factor for the e-bike.*{color} Based on the UX survey people seem to appreciate e-bikes which feel like ordinary pedal bikes.

Lacing spokes will not cost more than *50.-* per work (not per hour). Rim costs about *17.-*. Not more than that. Spokes cost depends on the type. Thicker type is about 3times more expensive than a thin 2mm spokes. 2mm is ordinary spoke diameter used on non-electric bikes. E-bike spokes are 2.4, 2.6, 3mm and cost much more therefore. Spokes will be custom-made if they need to be shortened and machined. Work could even be done {{2024-07-23}} .

To clarify, it is lights & dynamo together which must be compliant according to ISO 6742-4, if we want to be ISO 4210 compliant in the end, as this is a supplement to the ISO 4210 which handles lights & retro-reflective devices.

!image-20240621-121024.png|width=100%,alt="image-20240621-121024.png"!

----

h3. Going into detail of the standard ISO 6742-4 and relevant chapters with explanations:

*3.4* - Since we specify the one & only combination of hub-dynamo & lights, we can consider that our system would be tested as a *Closed system*, which has easier-to-pass requirements, which are not component-based, but they are system-based, so must comply with the +combination of hub dynamo & lights that the manufacturer (in our case Bolt/LY) specifies+.

!image-20240621-112951.png|width=100%,alt="image-20240621-112951.png"!

----

*4.1* - this chapter shows which are the applicable requirement & test method chapters for both systems, open systems components & closed system in general. When it comes to MB1, the requirements are in chapters *4.2*, *4.3* and *6*, test methods are described in chapters *7.1*, *7.2* and *7.6*.

!image-20240621-120713.png|width=100%,alt="image-20240621-120713.png"!

----

*4.2*, *4.3*, *7.1*, *7.2* - these chapters are general corrosion & water resistance tests which the lights/dynamo combination needs to pass. These are tests which will be done during vehicle compliance testing for the hub dynamo/lights system:

!image-20240621-120630.png|width=100%,alt="image-20240621-120630.png"!

----

*6* - this chapter describes more specific requirements for the closed system (lights/dynamo combination). Moreover, it says exact photometrical performance requirement at different speeds.

!image-20240621-121543.png|width=100%,alt="image-20240621-121543.png"!

----

*7.6* - this chapter describes more specific tests for the closed system (lights/dynamo combination) which will be done during. These are tests which will be done during vehicle compliance testing for the hub dynamo/lights system:

!image-20240621-121748.png|width=100%,alt="image-20240621-121748.png"!

h2. Conclusion

Dynamo itself must not have ISO 6742-4 compliance, as it applies for the whole system (either closed/open), but there are specific tests for open system which only covers the hub dynamo, which in our case is not required, but would be nice to know if they are still pre-compliant. In our case, we need to determine that our selected (& not interchangeable) components are harmonically compliant with ISO 6742-4 steps described above, if/when the vehicle will go for ISO 4210 certification in the future.

h2. *Compliance*

To be completely compliant with our MB1, we need to comply (on component basis & vehicle basis) with the following standards:

* *Vehicle level*
** ISO 4210:2023 - “_Cycles - safety requirements for bicycles_“ (all subchapters)
* *Component level*
** Lights (front & rear)
*** ISO 6742-1 “_Cycles - Lighting and retro-reflective devices - Part 1: Lighting and light signaling devices_“
*** ISO 6742-4 “_Cycles - Lighting and retro-reflective devices - Part 4: Lighting systems powered by the cycle's movement_” ({color:#bf2600}_questionable whether required on light basis_{color})
** Reflectors (side reflectors, reflectors integrated into lights)
*** ISO 6742-2 “_Cycles - Lighting and retro-reflective devices - Part 2: Retro-reflective devices_”
** Hub dynamo
*** ISO 6742-4 “_Cycles - Lighting and retro-reflective devices - Part 4: Lighting systems powered by the cycle's movement_”
** *StVZO is also good for all components, to be DE compliant!*

h2. *Lights*

Currently the selected lights are from *Sate-lite*, lights are *same as Dragon/Cobra scooters*. There are multiple reasons for using these components

{color:#006644}*Good*{color}*:*

* They are ISO 6742-1 and ISO 6742-2 compliant (standalone lights & reflectors standards required for compliance.
** Also good - StVZO compliant for German markets!
* They have a broad working DC voltage range (6V - 58V).
* They are hub dynamo compatible.
* We can use exact same components as we use for *Dragon/Cobra* *without modification*.
* The supplier is validated & we have a good relationship with them!

{color:#ff5630}*Need to specify*{color}*:*

* The lights are not yet ISO 6742-4 certified exactly, but that is yet to be determined whether they need standalone certification.

h2. *Hub Dynamo*

Currently there are two models which are under consideration, one is from Shimano (much less likely to be selected), and Karasawa (very likely to be selected).

Requirements for the Dynamo:

* Must have sufficient power output for powering two lights constantly.
* Must have a voltage regulator (either integrated or standalone) to limit voltage to a safe range, and also ensure that we are not using high AC voltage (or VDC RMS) in the system which supplies power to the lights.
* Must be ISO 6742-4 compliant

Currently we still need to validate the lights with the dynamos we plan to use, but preliminary testing with Shimano Nexus 6V 3W hub (on our Arcade bicycle sample) proved that the lights can work well with the dynamo, *even if there is no voltage regulator installed*!

* [~accountid:5eb363355862510b794e3507] checked with the labs in China and none of them can do ISO6742-4 for the dynamos. According to the labs [~accountid:5eb363355862510b794e3507] spoke to, the ISO6742-4 is not needed. 
* [~accountid:5e4658b55a495e0c91a7a011] to double check if the ISO6742 is needed.

The task can be moved to “Done”, as from me no more actions are to be taken from the task.

h3. Targets & results:

* *_Define compliance requirements (tests & reports) which are required to be compliant as a vehicle for both lights and hub dynamo._* - We have determined that we need to be compliant with ISO4210 with the entire vehicle, so the lights must be compliant with ISO6742-1, reflectors (even integrated) must be compliant with ISO6742-2, and the harmonized hub dynamo-lights working logic is specified in ISO6742-4. Installation instructions are according to according to ISO6742-3 or manufacturers guidelines if specified that way in the standard. Our hub dynamo & lights combination is tested at Sate-lite & confirmed to work in a compliant way, so certification should not be an issue.
* *_Make sure that the selected lights and hub dynamo work well together on the vehicle._* - As per last item, pre-compliance & functionality tests have been done at Sate-lite & components work according to standard (as expected).
* *_Define components, positioning & cabling logic on a more simplistic level, so that the majority of responsibility would be on Longuye (we say how we want it done, and they will follow our general guidelines)._* - positioning is according to the cable tree & 3D (somewhat still open due to engineering solutions which are not 100% agreed), but the general idea of how lights must be positioned is in place. *Cable lengths will be specified by Bolt, not Longuye!*

h2. Conclusion

The proof of concept has passed, the parts are compatible to one-another. The solar panel provides just enough voltage & current to keep the battery charged to some extent. The OMNI OC30 smart lock charging circuit is able to work adequately in cooperation with the solar panel, meaning that the voltage is regulated well enough to safely charge the battery even if the solar panel voltage/current fluctuates significantly on some occasions.

h3. Next steps

After BE implementation of the OMNI OC30 smart lock, we shall evaluate the capacity of the battery & tune the BE<->IOT communication so that battery usage is optimal & IOT is able to operate normally while using the least possible amount of energy.

Tests shall be done without the solar panel to evaluate the current battery capacity, and then with the solar panel to see how we are able to prolong the battery capacity with the aid of the solar panel.

1) I received 2 batteries from Germany to test this issue: 1 of the batteries sent was TechSum C2 battery which is not related and the otherone was TWS C2 battery which did NOT have this problem.

2) I tried to replicate the error but it did not occur as the problem is related to the INITIAL “lock” state of the battery.

In general, if a new battery is inserted into the scooter and it reports battery lock 0 (Max discharge allowed more than 0.5A), the IoT does not send “unlock” command to the BMS. The actual state of the battery is actually 1 (discharge up to 0.5A is allowed).
If this state is toggled by using the PC tool, the bug is removed.

3) The bug occurs in TWS factory when the SN is flashed to the BMS. If the lock state at the flashing moment is incorrect, then this bug occurs. - I spoke to Kevin about this and he will contact TWS to get more clarification on this from them on {{2022-07-20}} .

4) New firmware sets the initial lock state to 1, So it does get synced with the actual lock value after the firmware is flashed, so that the IoT will send the unlock command to the battery.

# The condition to change the 'Locked' state of the TWS BMS and Bolt protocol
1.1 V20 and earlier FW
A. BMS protocol Locked state is changed from 0 to 1 when communication timeout exceeds  30S or Bolt protocol write command writes 1( BMS Locked state will be changed to 1 synchronously )
B. BMS protocol Locked state is changed from 1 to 0 when Bolt protocol write command writes 0（BMS Locked state will be changed to 0 synchronously）
C. Bolt protocol Locked state is changed from 0 to 1 when Bolt protocol write command writes 1 or BMS  changed from 0 to 1( Bolt protocol Locked state will be synchronously changed to 1 )
D. Bolt protocol Locked state is changed from 1 to 0 when Bolt protocol write command writes 0 or TWS protocol writes SN what causes the Bolt protocol Locked sate is initialized to 0
# Why does burning SN cause this problem?
A. Bolt protocol will also read the SN code, so writing SN requires synchronously updating the SN code read by Bolt protocol. Updating the SN is through the unified initialization interface. In this
way, Bolt protocol Locked state will also be set to 0, while BMS Locked sate is still 1
# Why don't all batteries have this problem
A. For V20 and earlier FW, Bolt protocol Locked state and BMS Locked state may be out of sync. The Locked state can be synchronized by Bolt protocol  writing command, and the battery will return to normal.
B. As long as BMS is updated or IOT sends unlock command twice, Bolt protocol Locked state and BMS Locked state will resume synchronization.
C. C1 batteries don't have this kind of situation, because all C1 scooters had experienced upgrading BMS and controllers before launch, Bolt protocol Locked state and BMS Locked state resumed synchronization.
D. During the internal test of TWS, the update function of some batteries had be tested, so for these batteries, Bolt protocol Locked state and BMS Locked state resumed synchronization.
# Why can't this fault be repeated when rolling back from V22 to V20
Please refer to 3.A and 3.D, as long as the BMS is updated or receives unlock command twice in a row, the state will resume synchronization.
# What has been modified in V22 firmware
The new firmware V22 synchronizes the BMS Locked state to the Bolt protocol Locked state in real-time, and retains the Bolt protocol Locked write command to change the BMS Locked state synchronously;

Define & Verify Root Cause
When we removed the limit of high-current discharge of the battery through PC, the battery can work normally on
the scooter. So it can be judged that the battery was in the limit state of high-current discharge, that was, the battery
did not receive the command from IOT to remove the limit of high-current discharge.
It can be seen from the load that when the discharge current exceeded 600mA, the battery started the protection
and forbids output. However, through PC can see that the Locked command of battery was in unlocked state.
IOT detected that the Locked command of battery was 0, so it did not send the unlock command to the battery.
However, the actual state of the battery was locked, which was not synchronized with the Locked command. As a
result, the battery cannot output with large current.

I made a prototype C1 battery with wire to wire connectors to check whether this solution is retrofittable into the current batteries.

Here is what I noted:

* Connector wires soldered onto the PCB have to make 180deg turn, therefore they have extreme bending radiuses.
* The connectors must be fitted above the PCB components - during assembly or with vibration those may be damaged
* some connectors and wires will come in contact with the mosfet heat-sink. In the worst case, if the heatsink gets hot, the connectors may melt.
* It is difficult to control the final position of the connectors and they can not be fixed inside the casing in a good way
* Requires precise wire lengths - The wire lengths may be different on the TWS and TechSum battery, because the connector may have to be placed differently.

I would avoid the retrofit solution mainly due to the possible damage to PCB, bad wire bending radiuses and wires and connectors being in contact with the heat sink.

For “upgrade version” we could possibly install the connectors on the PCB which help to avoid the bending radiuses, helps to fix the connectors well enough and avoids the connectors and wires being in contact with the heat sink.

Overview of the connector:

# The contact is split into 3 pieces and because of that the width of the contact surface is very small - 1.6mm. This may cause extra wearing on the contact surface.

!image-20220916-052401.png|width=1342,height=1091!

2. Upper ends of the female pins are really nicely protected - impossible to bend the contact. This small plastic edge over the end of the pin gives also extra contact force to the male pin. 

!image-20220916-052844.png|width=926,height=879!

3. The bottom part is fixed with 2 screws - not ultrasonic welded or glued. My suggestion is to sealed the connector from back side - the easiest way could be potting h=2mm because then we can seal also the areas around the pins.

|!image-20220916-053727.png|width=33.33333333333333%!|!image-20220916-053919.png|width=33.33333333333333%!|

4. There are 2 small pins that allow to install the connector only one way

!image-20220916-072458.png|width=41.66666666666667%!

5. Thickness of the pin is only 1mm - I think it is not enough to last 5 years on a street. Thicker pin needs wider connector

!image-20220916-073007.png|width=41.66666666666667%!

6. It seems that there should be a gasket between the female and male sides but the part is not in 3D model - there should be a gasket or maybe the gasket should be bigger and outside the connector so that it will cover the female connector 100% when we connect the connectors.

!image-20220916-075632.png|width=1674,height=1056!

7. These double pins could be used as a backup pins to secure the connection

8. There is no floating function

yes, for testing 1 set is enough.

However I am slightly concerned on the safety of those RISINGSUN tires. There is no steel wire in the bead, which means that the tire can stretch over the rim edge during cornering. We have seen the same thing happening with OKAI a couple of times and their rim profile is way better for this kind of stretchy tires. Our rim has the V-shaped groove in the middle, which doesnt support the tire that well. If we decide to move forward with those dog toy style tires we must do a lab test to check how much sideways pressure can be applied on the tire before it pops off the rim bead.



For the PU filled tires - Is it 100% certain that the PU foam cannot be installed through the valve stem hole after the tire is mounted on the rim? It seems to be similar to expanding construction foam/PUR insulation foam, only way denser. I dont see why it shouldnt be possible to install it through the valve stem hole, it would then expand inside the tire and harden?

The specification of the TVS diode is 5A, and the locked rotor current of the lock will not exceed 2A, which is more than 2.5 times the margin.
Both Genfo and Bolt schemes use TVS to absorb the back electromotive force of inductive loads. If the TVS breakdown problem is not considered, both schemes are fine.
However, if TVS breakdown is considered, the risk of the Bolt solution is that the short-circuit current will pass through the MOS of the upper bridge, short-circuiting 5V, and the upper bridge will be damaged. The short-circuit current of Genfo's scheme does not pass through the MOS of the upper bridge.

From the design point of view, the 5A diode is large enough, and from the test results, it is not the large current that damages the chip, but the large voltage.

So the question is already considering using a large enough diode, should we also consider the risk of diode breakdown？

Cell voltage difference >= 300mV for more than 20 seconds - This threshold may be easily met in old batteries or high current discharges.

* With Techsum so far it seems to be not a problem? Tho when batteries get older, for sure we need to monitor it, to not start getting false positives. 
** Rough calculation from previous capacity / energy test for techsum battery. Let`s assume we have 300mV cell difference. It means at least one cell (300mV lower than others) operational range will be 2,7V-3,85V (charge cut 4,15V for other cells). Charged battery energy will max 80% compared to balanced cell battery (maybe more like 70% even, because no saturation charging, current will not drop before charge cut). It shows how important it is to keep cells balanced. Just for info.

 We recommend keeping the V22 full charge protection. MaxCellVol>4.125V & charging current (100mA~300mA) & 5s.

* This seems to not limit charging voltage, when current is above 300mA

HengBen had our previous 3D model where I wanted to use the metal springs on the sides and they sent their feedback based on that model.

Feedback from HengBen:

*Lower cap:*

* Area around the spring pin is too thin and the plastic may brake too easily
* Minimum draft angle is *0.5 degrees* with regular mould
* It is possible to have *0 degreed* in case we have a complex mould with extra sliders - mould cost will be *2.5x higher* (today we do not have any quotations jet so we do not know the real cost of the mould)
* With 0 degrees draft angle the unit cost also goes up about *1.2 RMB* because they have to use bigger injection machine (mould will be bigger and small machine can not be used anymore)
* It is ok to use our plastic alloy with *0 degrees* draft angle

*Upper cap:*

* At the moment the sides have too big wall thickness and there will be shrinkages on the top and side surfaces - need to get rid of that extra material. Need to change the visual
* Injection nut standard maximum length is 12mm. It is possible to have longer nut but then it must be customized (MOQ 20…30k).
* The top surface of the injection nut must be on the same level with the material (can not be lower in the material)

Bolt-Genfo-Satellite（STLT） 3-party diagnosis

We organized STLT to diagnose these bad lights in Genfo factory. The three parties reached a consensus and signed the conclusion of this diagnosis.

Preliminary Cause Analysis

# The 7005 chip of the light is broken by the big voltage that is from the controller
# The controller causes overcurrent and hiccup protection due to damage to the light chip. Then the current limiting resistor  is broken down as the hiccup protection is triggered.

Root Cause Analysis

# Controller-They did not  consider that the surge current of the light is relatively large, and sufficient protection is not made at the output end of the controller, resulting in the breakdown of the current limiting resistor.
# When a scooter is running with a  full battery and downhill. The potential on MBEMF is superimposed on the VCC terminal, the battery will not absorb the voltage, and the voltage is greater than the chip voltage limit of the light, causing the chip to break down, triggering hiccup protection, and current limiting resistor breakdown.
# Light-Due to the unstable chip of some lights, the surge current is too high and the duration exceeds the normal value at the moment of power-on.

Improvements

# Controller-Change the chip resistor to a common resistor, and connect a current limiting resistor in series. Software optimization, when the output voltage of the lamp is greater than 53V, the PWM will be turned off within 64us to protect the output circuit
# Light-Increase the chip voltage of the light to 100V Min, and connect a current limit resistor to input end.
# The light supplier will use high voltage to do the FQC 100%.
# Improve the waterproof

The first test with vertical positioning and 2 batteries per slot was {color:#bf2600}*unsuccessful*{color}. 

*Key takeaways:*

* The most crucial weaknesses of this solution/test were:
** Close proximity of other batteries
*** Vertically more important than horizontally, but in the end both matter.
*** The fire always shoots upwards while burning, and in the report it will be apparent that after the initial thermal runaway of the fire source, the bottom batteries were cooking the top ones from both ends, and the proximity allowed for a very quick temperature transfer between the fire source and surrounding batteries (sides & most importantly top)
** Two batteries per slot
*** It is crucial to note that the fire spreading to any other slot (except for the fire source slot) happened only after both of the batteries in the fire source slot had burned in a massive flame. It is highly likely that the outburst of energy from two batteries per slot caused the chain reaction.
** Both aforementioned issues simultaneously
*** The two factors together made it possible for the temperature to reach such a high temperature, that after all the batteries above the fire source column had finished burning, slots on both sides also started the thermal runaway process. *It did not happen from flames melting plastic*, but just large temperatures in the fire source surrounding area. Initially, we thought that the middle column had burned and test was finished, but minutes later the batteries on the sides started smoking and started exploding/burning violently.

The OMNI ring lock samples {color:#bf2600}*FAILED*{color} functionality validation.

During live testing, rides were done on uneven terrain, over bumps and vibration-triggering surfaces. After multiple live tests on the street, the outcome was always the same - lock was not functional after 1-3 orders (short orders - 4-6 minutes per order, less than 1 km):

* 4/5 times, it was not possible to unlock the lock after the final order
* 1/5 times, it was not possible to lock the lock after the final order

Upon further investigation, it was discovered that the lock actuator (motor + metal plate) was getting stuck in a position, where the lock was reporting that it was “OPEN” (although it was clearly not), and the motor was not moving whatsoever.

After the tests, the vehicle was taken to HQ basement, lock disassembled, and following was discovered:

!lock issue.png|width=100%!

The motor cam lobe was getting stuck in this unconventional position. In this position, if the motor is not manipulated (stress from mechanical parts was aleviated), it will not start working at all. Only solution to get the motor moving again is to slightly rotate the motor so that it would start reporting “CLOSED” position. Only then did the lock work normally again.

+*IMPORTANT NOTE:*+ We tried stress-testing the lock next to the vehicle (hitting it against ground surface, hitting it with a hammer) multiple times repeatedly while locking-unlocking the lock, and we were unable to recreate the issue. Currently it only happens when the vehicle is ridden on the streets.

+*IMPORTANT NOTE 2:*+ We validated, that CANBUS communication was good, that there were no cables damaged and all connectors were connected each and every time.

!lock issue.mp4|width=720,height=1280!

Popping another thought here:

* Currently our logic in the Charger app flow is that Local OPS must report something when the vehicles are collected, faulty, and need to be put to “Waiting for service”. The thing is, these current (and new ones as well) are very specific things to report, and a driver/operator/3PL battery swapper can *never* be as accurate as possible here, thus the usage of some random items to put it to the correct state. Reporting items and solutions can not be the same thing, as you *can not pre-diagnose the vehicle just by looking at it!* At the same time, same phenomena might have different solutions (e.g. in Cobra case, lights issues can be related to either a faulty light unit, a cable issue or even the controller light circuit, how is an operator supposed to report the remotely correct thing).
** *_Solution_*: Make a separate list of reportable issues as phenomenas/behaviours/easily described issues with the vehicle, and keep the “maintenance issues” as “solutions”, not something anyone can just report.

# Evacuation of the cabinet from the building (refer to operation manual); the escape routes must be unobstructed

Some more info from Denios:


* In general, you should consider that in case of a fire of a battery inside the cabinet:
** Other batteries can be affected (a metal sheet between the batteries won´t make any difference for example)
** The cabinet most probably won´t be usable after the fire and most probable not possible to re-build it. The cabinets fire resistance is based on fire tests and if there is a real fire inside the cabinet probably many elements will be damaged so it is not possible to re-build it and certify the fire resistance again.  
** The suppressor is not an extinguisher. It blocks the reaction for around 30 minutes so that you can have time to activate your emergency plan, call the fire brigade, evacuate people etc…

 

IT IS IMPORTANT that you understand that the whole cabinet design is based on AVOIDING the fires to happen. Thanks to the different alarm levels and the communication extra devices, the cabinet purpose is to inform you in case of anything happen (temperature increase for example) so that you can act quickly and avoid the batteries to increase the damage and explode/set on fire. It is also important that you define a proper emergency plan for each cabinet level of alarm so that you can act quickly and safely avoiding risks and more problematic damages.

So the problem is that the potting material has low viscosity when it is mixed and it runs through small openings. I don’t know what is the initial potting compounds that Incap used but I can give my comments based on the options. For your reference, the potting material we use in China has 1500±500 mPa.s viscosity, the other option had 2000±500 mPa.s and the one that we use here for RFIDs has 2000mPa.s when it is mixed. So this is the range that it works well. 

# *NP1173* has *10000mPa.s* viscosity when it is mixed. It will solve the problem but it is a bit thick that it may not be able to penetrate between the cells and small openings. 
# *NP1024* has *2000mPa.s* viscosity when it is mixed. This is quite good to try. It also has a lower density than the first one. Also, it has UL 94 V-0 level flame retardancy. One thing that I didn’t like about this one is the hardness. It gets Shore D 50-55 harness level which is hard comparing the potting materials that we use. It needs to be tested. It might create too much tension on the components. 
# *NP1172* has *4000mPa.s* viscosity when it is mixed. This is also good to try. It has a lower density that the second option, 1.13 specific gravity. Soft and has no stress on electrical components. 
# *NP1192* has *4000mPa.s* viscosity when it is mixed. It has 1.13 specific gravity as the previous one. Soft and has no stress on electrical components. 
# *NP5005* has *500mPa.s* viscosity when it is mixed. It might be still runny. But it has low specific gravity of 0.95. It might be quite soft that we cannot use. 

So *option 3* *and 4* seems good to try. If they have, we can try option 2 as well but it might be a risky one in the long term as we don’t know how it will react to temperature changes.

	- Removing the battery compartment
	- Connecting the main power harness and routing the cable
	- Adding heat shrink tubing on the cables
	- Refitting battery compartment
	- Attn!!! BATTERY MUST NOT BE INSIDE DURING THIS PROCESS!
	- Removing Display & keypad from handlebar
		- Cutting away the keypad cable with instructions
	- Releasing all cables for upfitting
	- Adjusting the handlebar

*Part 3: Cable lock installation*
	- Remove rear light bracket from vehicle
	- Remove rear light from vehicle
	- Remove existing ringlock
	- Fasten the cable lock to the bracket
	- Attach the assembly to the vehicle
	- Route the cables properly through the bicycle
	- Refit controller cover

*Part 4: Security fasteners*
	- Refit left crank arm
	- Remove crank arm bolts and replace them with Penta+ Security nuts from OKAI eBikes
	- Refit left crank arm
	- Check tension for front hub nuts and add front hub covers.
	- Check tension for rear hub nuts and add rear hub covers.

	- Install the lower plastic - attaching the IOT lower plastic, lower plastic lid and mounting brackets
	- Install the IOT external board and connect the cables
	- Install the IOT to the external board
	- Assemble IOT compartment
	- Create the vehicle in Admin
	- Insert battery
	- Test the vehicle in Admin

	- Install the pedals

* Wall between batteries
** Most suppliers do not have it in default set-up, CN suppliers offered it as custom solution
*** We could ask for the walls or add them ourselves.
**** Adding these walls, we might lose the warranty since we would be modifying the default cabinet
***** Fire tests, etc were done without the walls
** Having walls, we could possibly reduce the number of batteries lost in case of a fire
* Smoke exhaust and fire suppressing. According to supplier feedback it is either one or the other.
** Since fire suppressing is most effective in a closed room, but smoke exhaust means there is ventilation. (NB\! Claimed by 2 suppliers that the fire could not be extinguished any way, we can just reduce the intensity)
*** Most cases the ventilation hole is the only place which could be used as a smoke exhaust, although the ventilation is shut off in case of a fire - so the effectiveness is reduced.
*** Options
**** Shall we just accept the reduced effectiveness of fire suppressant?
**** Shall we mark the suppressant as “optional”?
**** Do we want to have suppressant  in our cabinets?
***** Could reduce the cost of the cabinet
***** Need to keep in mind that by reducing the fire intensity we could save some adjacent batteries as well.

h3. Testing:

Did further testing remotely with Karlsruhe mechanics, and we came to a conclusion.

If the testing is done in the following order - the IOT manages to connect to the server.

# Attach the IOT to a vehicle in ADMIN V2
# Check/activate the SIM card in Admin
## Before proceeding to step 3, wait up to 1 h for the SIM status in the Admin to turn to “LIVE”
### It can not be “PENDING/LIVE” or “OFF”
# Plug the IOT to the scooter
## The scooter battery must not be *completely empty* nor *completely full*, charging must commence, charger must power controller & battery to activate the IOT from transportation mode.
# Wait 30 seconds
# Plug the charger to the vehicle (controller, not directly to the battery)
# The IOT should now activate properly and everything should work correctly.



There was also noted on BE side authentication failures related to passwords in our system - the issue likely came from the fact that all IOTs entered to our DB prior to the beginning of 2024 were done through the old PHP Admin, where the logic automatically configured the correct password for NB IOTs, but the new Admin system does not. Keijo fixed this issue and deployed the password overwriting for all new IOTs added from the last batch {{2024-03-13}}.

h3. Solution

To mitigate this issue, locals have been also instructed to follow the guidelines as written in the [slack message|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CTN1HV5D0/p1714467447443679?thread_ts=1710324211.301709&cid=CTN1HV5D0]:

!image-20240430-115319.png|width=75%,alt="image-20240430-115319.png"!

h3. Root cause

The root cause of non-connectivity was caused due to multiple bad conditions overlapping, all of which impact one another:

* *Unclear IOT activation procedure* - NB proprietary IOTs need to be woken up in a certain way (IOT plugged to scooter, charger attached to controller soon after), so they would “wake up” from their transportation low-energy deactivated state. If done incorrectly (or not at all), the IOT will just go back to sleep.
* *SIM opening delay* - most IOTs, which were tested, were already plugged in with the SIM card in the OFF state. This is a bad habit in general. Even if the IOT manages to activate, the modem will probably fail to connect to the server due to the SIM activation being under way/SIM just being OFF still, and the result of that is large time delays for the IOT watchdog to reboot the modem and eventually connect to the server in a proper manner
* (_Secondary_) *Admin V2 IOT creation logic (un)knowledgeability* - old (PHP) Admin was used until the beginning of 2024 to add new NB IOTs to the system. Whereas the old Admin used to configure the credentials for these NB IOTs itself automatically, it did not do it for Admin V2. These IOTs need a specific password (“nbiot”) to be saved as their credentials in order to connect it to Bolt BE, otherwise it will constantly fail authentication and just sleep. This was solved as mentioned above.

h3. Learning points

* For 3rd party proprietary IOTs (Such as OKAI, NB, HJ etc.) we should have always proper instructions/procedures on how to activate them without issues.
* SIM opening must be more clearly understandable to LOPS who replace IOTs, as large time delays/general confusion will happen due to the SIMs being “OFF” and vehicles trying to come online, which in itself can cause issues and misdiagnosed DOA IOTs.

Genfo informational pdf:

Question 1：
The motor will not lock when the speed of the scooter is greater than 11KM/H.
Reason：
In previous firmware, for security reasons, there was a logic that did not lock the motor for speeds
greater than 11KM/H.
Solution:
Remove the speed criteria.


Question 2：
Scooter will accelerate when somebody jumps on scooter, when wheel is locked ( possible in forward
and backward direction).
Reason：
The controller has the motor positive and negative code self - learning. The force when locking the
motor is related to the offset Angle of the motor. When the scooter is stationary, the force of locking the
motor is 0. When jumping on the scooter suddenly, the Angle of the motor will be forcibly changed by a
large Angle, and the controller will think that the positive and negative codes of the motor are wrong and
learn a wrong code. When the motor code is incorrectly learned, the motor will turn itself half a turn and
learn the correct code back, this is why the motor accelerates.
Solution:
Remove self-learning function when motor locks.


Question 3：
Accelerate the increase of regenerative braking force when locking the motor, and increase the force to
the maximum within 1s.
Solution:
Increase the PWM percentage of EABS to the maximum within 1s.

The first test with vertical positioning and 2 batteries per slot was {color:#bf2600}*unsuccessful*{color}.

*Key takeaways:*

* The most crucial weaknesses of this solution/test were:
** Close proximity of other batteries
*** Vertically more important than horizontally, but in the end both matter.
*** The fire always shoots upwards while burning, and in the report it will be apparent that after the initial thermal runaway of the fire source, the bottom batteries were cooking the top ones from both ends, and the proximity allowed for a very quick temperature transfer between the fire source and surrounding batteries (sides & most importantly top)
** Two batteries per slot
*** It is crucial to note that the fire spreading to any other slot (except for the fire source slot) happened only after both of the batteries in the fire source slot had burned in a massive flame. It is highly likely that the outburst of energy from two batteries per slot caused the chain reaction.
** Both aforementioned issues simultaneously
*** The two factors together made it possible for the temperature to reach such a high temperature, that after all the batteries above the fire source column had finished burning, slots on both sides also started the thermal runaway process. *It did not happen from flames melting plastic*, but just large temperatures in the fire source surrounding area. Initially, we thought that the middle column had burned and test was finished, but minutes later the batteries on the sides started smoking and started exploding/burning violently.
* In total, *we lost 12 batteries to the fire to thermal runaway, and more due to long high-temperature exposeure and mechanical damages (melting)*

HW team visited Ilvestments workplaces for repairing batteries, where we monitored battery repairs being done on a regular basis. We described the processes in very accurate detail and timed most of the processes. There were two processes - C1 nickel repair and C1 BMS repair which we could not time, but we agreed with Ilvestments, that they would film the entire process for each procedure from scratch, and time the process for 10 batteries (for each process), to get the average time per battery (as the process is never done 1 battery at a time, always in batches of ~10 at least for optimization).

*Key takeaways from the visit:*

* The procedures that Ilvestments uses in their daily battery repairs, are very well optimized. Together with the engineers, we could not find almost any room for optimization in their processes, neither could we come up with any suggestions to improve their working methods or processes.
* The working methods are on a very high level, and output is extremely high.
* The only slight improvement we could make, is to have the lower caps come pre-assembled from CN.
** This opens up a new set of problems, as the assembled caps are not the same for different manufacturers and models, so more inventory items will need to be introduced and tracked.
* No pricing negotiations were done yet, but Ilvestments implied that there is no point in wandering around the topic and they think it is very fair if we want to discuss the pricing.
** In our favor, there is the fact of increased prices since the updated pricing method
** In our favor, there is the fact that the processes for their battery repairs are very optimized and their work pace is very high.
** In our favor, we found that the current price we pay as extra for each and every lower cap assembly, is excessive, and this does not currently justify itself.
** Their main topic of pricing negotiations from their side, is that we can discuss prices in different ways, and we could potentially find a way to decrease costs to our liking, but Bolt would need to ensure a regular and fixed inflow of broken batteries in that case.
** Ilvestments proposed an idea of fixed price for a single battery in case of C1 and C2, whatever the repair. *NB!* This was just brought up as an idea from them, but the prices were not discussed and no calculations for this have been made!

Because damage to end cap happens because there is need to get batteries out, and batteries don’t have no handle and is fixed with Velcro and therefor notable force is required. For the mechanics it is easiest to use end cap as leverage point because there is not much space from where it would be possible to remove battery.
So if we modify end cap so that it is strong enough and let them to use pry bars to remove battery then we may just re-locate the problem - since controller or frame is used as leverage point and these could be new risk areas which may get damaged during battery removal.

“We had a 4 hour session logging/diagnosing the IOTs I had prepared beforehand with HJ sales manager Fiona, and HJ software engineer Mr. Wei.We checked multiple IOTs, and captured logs with a specific device and a specific program.

From these logs - we saw during investigation, that the old SIMs cards (these, which were inside from the factory) were not connecting to our BE. Once we swapped the SIM cards to known good ones, they worked. From the logs collected, HJs conclusion was that it was a SIM card issue.Later, all of the IOTs that we replced with known good SIM, and replaced again with old one, everything worked well, which is super strange.

Our BE and IOT teams joined me in looking at the logs and diagnosing further IOTs later by ourselves with the tool, and with the data we found, we do not think it has anything to do with the SIM whatsoever.

We will compile everything we found, and everything we attempted to do in some document.

Ultimately - we will submit our findings to HJ, ask them about what they could do to make the situation better. Whether they understand/acknowledge the issue, is to be seen. They seemed quite adamant today that the SIM cards were the root cause, but our team is leaning towards another direction.Best outcome today was that we got the device to capture modem logs from HongJi IOTs, so that we can finally investigate what is happening more in depth.

Remarks: 

* GSM quality is not great, but above average. IOT did not lose connection once. AVG value is 19 (out of 32). More than expected considering the location of the IOT, but it would be good if the values were much larger since conditions were perfect (Cobra scooter would achieve near perfect signal quality values during this test).
