We had an initial meeting with Quectel regarding the engraved antenna in plastic. This method could eliminate using extra GNSS and LTE antenna and have it embedded in plastic. 

This solution could avoid one cable routing as well which is GNSS antenna cable. 

Also, one layer PCBA could be used - this would give us enough height to have 2nd plastic for waterproofing and skip using potting material. New plastic has to be made for this version. 

The 3D model is sent to Quectel for evaluation {{2024-05-07}}

{color:#ff5630}*Additional BOM parts:* {color}

In order to achieve this following parts are needed: 

* 2nd plastic part (new mold) which will enclose the assembly 
* O-ring sealing or overmold gasket around the 2nd plastic to make the casing airtight 
* Grommets around the cable
** GPS co-axial cable 
** Speaker cable
** Back-up battery cable
** IoT power cable
** AI module cable
* Breathing valve on the 2nd plastic
* Glue

Also: 

* Possible mold modification on the current IoT plastic or even a new mold



{color:#ff5630}*PROS:* {color}

* Removing the following parts from the assembly and process: 
** Potting compound 
** Potting and curing process
** After potting test
* Quick access to components on the PCBA if it fails. Higher chance to remove and replace components on the IoT PCBA
* Display PCBA or main PCBA could be replaced easier if one fails



{color:#ff5630}*CONS:*{color}

* As the potting material won’t be there, the IoT assembly will get weaker
** IoT will be more vulnerable to impacts and hits 
** The impacts from top plastic would crack the IoT enclosure and therefore it won’t be waterproof anymore



{color:#ff5630}*Alternative option:* {color}

* Ultrasonic welding on the IoT plastic and enclosure plastic - this would eliminate big modification on the IoT plastic. Also, we can skip using grommet or O-ring. The problem with this solution is it requires UW machine and additional machine + jigs cost. 
* In case of using UW machine, we might need to use pre-welding check and after welding check. We are in similar situation with pre-potting check and after potting check. 



{color:#ff5630}*Next step:*{color}

* Designing the case and get a precise mold and BOM cost. 
* Make an ROI calculation and make a decision if we want to refine the design and make initial reliability tests. 



{color:#ff5630}*Possible cost save in the current process:* {color}

* Eliminating either pre-potting test
** If the cost of pre-potting test bigger than failing rate cost then cancel this step

SOC start - from previous log, SOC when ride started, IOT log has same data

SOC end - from previous log, SOC when ride ended, IOT log has same data

SOC drop = SOC start - SOC end

distance \[m] - ride distance from previous log

SOC calc by voltage, in start - I needed something to compare BMS SOC, based on one of my previous tests, I tried to calculate SOC based on battery voltage, when idle time has been at least 15min. I will post SOC calculation sheet here, tab- “SOC calc”, enter battery voltage into - “Voltage:” (thick border cell). Base test to create this was: discharge full cobra battery - 15min 2A, then 15min 0,03A, … . With 15 min voltage seems to stabilize and battery capacity for every stabilized moment can be calculated. This way battery capacity in scooter idle could be calculated based on battery voltage. Seems this calculation is far from BMS SOC but still this method has potential for BMS accuracy validation remotely in my opinion - would need to get results with exactly the same battery and with different temperatures (logging with electrical load). * *Most of the components' location has changed on the PCB*
* Most of the routing was re-done

* *Added 100nF capacitors: C26, C32, C39, C41*
* *Added ferrite bead FB4*
* *Added 10k resistors: R38, R39, R40, R41, R42*
* *Added 2.2R resistors: R13, R14, R18, R36, R37*
* *Added eMMC U2*
* *Added 3V3 TVS D1*

* *P1 cable pinout changed.*
* *Removed following components:  C31, C22, C13, C29, F1, FB1, Q1, Q2, R23, R26, R20, R21, R22, R27, R28, R29, R33, D22*

Tested scenarios:

Helmet lock is connected and detected by IOT:
1. Backend tries to switch ai cable power off but since helmet lock is keeping ai cable power on the command is ignored
2. Backend sends ai cable power restart command and IOT toggles ai cable power for 1 second

Helmet lock is not connected:
1. Backend switches ai power on and off successfully
2. Backend sends ai cable power restart command and IOT toggles ai cable power for 1 second

When IOT tries to detect helmet lock it would power on the helmet lock for ~15 seconds. This can lead to a situation when AI module has enough time to boot file system thus abrupt power off can potentially damage the module. The quick fix for this problem is to keep AI module powered on even if helmet lock was not detected. In future we shall provide a more sophisticated algorithm for controlling AI module power.

Working with MMM data we have one check that ensures that assumptions hold (i.e. that trend is 0). 

This ensures that we do not have assumptions of the model broken as well as ensures we have no systematic error. 

It seems that in this regard, it might be interesting to look at error distribution of the model

Script that helped me look at the errors here: [https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/?o=3829506390716583#notebook/1928420349208250/command/1928420349208254|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/?o=3829506390716583#notebook/1928420349208250/command/1928420349208254]

*Ideal picture we should observe:*

* Model without cost has systematic errors where we have some changes in ads.
* Model with cost does not have systematic errors and its errors remind white noise.

The picture described above would be convincing that spend is actually explaining some parts of the model, where without ads we are not able to explain it.

Examples are:

* *Amsterdam* - visually very good model. Compensates error where it’s required (except Sep 2023 where we stopped user archival and current summer, where something weird is happening) 
!Amsterdam - Looking at error direction.png|width=22.621407333994053%,alt="Amsterdam - Looking at error direction.png"!
* *Madrid* - model also very well compensates error with Android spends in March’24

!Madrid - systematic error (possibly decreased effect).png|width=22.621407333994053%,alt="Madrid - systematic error (possibly decreased effect).png"!
* *Berlin* - some systematic error happening in Sep-Dec’23

!Berlin- example.png|width=33.33333333333333%,alt="Berlin- example.png"!



For this we would need not plot the MAPE (absolute error, like previously), but actually depict the error (with its sign).



Where to move next with this:

* Model selection (like the one with Robyn) instead of model prioring. 
** We could multiple generate models and evaluate them on multiple parameters, so that analyst could look at the picture of errors once we have all iterations complete and choose the most reasonable option (not necessarily automatically)
** I made a small prototype here:[https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/?o=3829506390716583#notebook/1736836351525837/command/1736836351525839|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/?o=3829506390716583#notebook/1736836351525837/command/1736836351525839]
** Note: iterating over multiple parameters can be frustrating. However, we can make the problem discrete (iterate over only vmax in [50,150,250]). The number of vmax-s is not infinite - e.g. we know that vmax most probably never exceeds 10-15% of overall signups (just because  it’s impossible that a channel brings more)
* Make some algorithm that would actually optimize not (not only) to general error reduction, but also to optimize for time-related systematic error (to make error as much white-noise as possible). {color:#ff5630}*<= Could this be some idea for a hackathon (even beyond MarTech)?*{color}



*Quick note:* Models actually not always need to be Bayesian. In the first option mentioned above (robyn-like model selection) we do not have actually to do anything Bayesian.

I will update new CAN spec version this week. Two new features:

* There will be a “hello world” msg that all CAN nodes must transmit upon MCU boot, with broadcast address
* Hatchlock does not need to implement the challenge-response, since no anti-theft settings defined. But it still needs to implement the HMAC-MD5, see next bullet..
* The firmware update will be protected with HMAC-MD5. Meaning that there will be 2 slots where IOT will write the HMAC-MD5 of the binary image and when FW_APPLY is received, then CAN node must also check the hash of the binary image. This ensures that 3rd party cannot update the fw (without knowing the shared secret)

Root cause of the problem was found by the lock supplier:

The potting compound was not completely cured because they immediately welded the cases with ultrasonic after filling the glue. The oxygen in the case was not enough to make the potting completely solidified, resulting in abnormal module behaviour. The have reworked 100pcs CAN models, all of which recovered to normal operation after potting cured.

As a temporary measure, they sent guys to rework, drill a hole in the case and allow the glue to be exposed to oxygen.

In the cycling world there are two main types of brake pad materials:

* organic pads (made out of kevlar, rubber, silica and resin) which offer better stopping performance in dry condition and less noise, however they are softer and more prone to wear
* Sintered (metallic) brake pads, that are pressed out of metallic dust. Those have a longer lifetime, but produce more brake dust and can be noisy. Also they work better in wet conditions.
* There are also some mixed organic+sintered compounds, but I have no experience with those. They are more expensive than either of the options above, but should be the ultimate mix of the two above.
